questions.title: Spring Data Redis Setup and Configuration
questions.question: How do you configure Spring Data Redis with Lettuce and what are the key configuration choices?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Lettuce vs Jedis: Lettuce is async, thread-safe, uses single connection; Jedis uses connection pool
- Spring Boot auto-configures Lettuce by default
- RedisTemplate: generic operations API — configured with serializers
- StringRedisTemplate: convenience template with String serializers
- Connection pooling: Lettuce with Commons Pool2 for connection pooling in production
- Sentinel and Cluster modes for HA/scale
- Serialization: GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer for objects, StringRedisSerializer for keys

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot auto-configures Lettuce as the Redis client by default. Lettuce is asynchronous and non-blocking — it uses a single connection shared across threads rather than a connection pool, which is more efficient for high-concurrency scenarios. For Spring's synchronous RedisTemplate, this still works fine because Lettuce handles multiplexing internally.

The most important configuration decision is serialization. By default, RedisTemplate uses Java serialization, which produces binary data that isn't human-readable and creates versioning issues if your classes change. Always configure explicit serializers — StringRedisSerializer for keys so they're readable in Redis CLI, and GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer for values so objects are stored as readable JSON.

For production, you'll also want connection pooling configured. Even though Lettuce uses one connection for pipelining, having a small pool allows multiple concurrent pipeline operations and provides reconnection resilience.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot auto-configures Lettuce as the Redis client by default.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Even though Lettuce uses one connection for pipelining, having a small pool allows multiple concurrent pipeline operations and provides reconnection resilience.

questions.title: RedisTemplate Operations in Depth
questions.question: How do you use RedisTemplate to perform complex Redis operations including pipelining and transactions?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- RedisTemplate.opsForValue(), opsForList(), opsForSet(), opsForZSet(), opsForHash()
- execute(RedisCallback): low-level access for complex commands
- Pipelining: batch multiple commands in one network round-trip — execute(pipelined=true)
- Transactions: MULTI/EXEC — executePipelined or execute with SessionCallback
- Lua scripts: RedisScript for atomic compound operations
- BoundKeyOperations: bind key once, perform multiple operations on it
- executePipelined: returns list of results from all commands

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
RedisTemplate provides operation objects for each Redis data type — opsForValue for strings, opsForList for lists, opsForSet for sets, and so on. Each gives you the full command set for that type with Java-friendly method names and automatic serialization handling.

Pipelining is a powerful optimization. Instead of sending each command individually and waiting for a response — each round-trip costing 1-5ms over the network — you batch multiple commands into a single network call and receive all responses at once. For loading or updating many keys at once, pipelining can reduce a 100ms operation to under 10ms.

Lua scripts give you atomic compound operations. Redis guarantees a Lua script runs atomically — no other commands can interrupt it. This is how you implement operations that require reading and conditionally writing without race conditions, like the check-and-release for distributed locks.

speakable_v2.hook: RedisTemplate provides operation objects for each Redis data type — opsForValue for strings, opsForList for lists, opsForSet for sets, and so on.

questions.title: Redis Pub/Sub and Messaging
questions.question: How does Redis pub/sub work and how do you implement it in a Spring Boot application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Redis pub/sub: fire-and-forget messaging — no persistence, no delivery guarantee
- Publisher: PUBLISH channel message; Subscriber: SUBSCRIBE channel
- Pattern subscribe: PSUBSCRIBE pattern* — subscribe with wildcard
- Use cases: real-time notifications, cache invalidation across instances, live events
- Spring: MessageListenerAdapter + RedisMessageListenerContainer
- Limitation: messages lost if subscriber is down — use Redis Streams for durability
- Redis Streams (XADD, XREAD, XGROUP): persistent, consumer groups, like Kafka

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget messaging. Publishers send messages to a channel, and all active subscribers on that channel receive them immediately. The key limitation is no persistence — if a subscriber is down when a message is published, that message is lost forever. This makes pub/sub appropriate for real-time notifications where missing an occasional message is acceptable, but not for reliable event processing.

A great use case for pub/sub is cache invalidation in a distributed application. When one instance updates a record and clears its local cache, it publishes a cache-invalidate message. All other instances are subscribed and immediately invalidate their own caches for that key. This keeps caches consistent across instances without a central coordination mechanism.

For reliable messaging, Redis Streams is the better choice. Streams persist messages and support consumer groups, so messages are only acknowledged after successful processing, missed messages can be replayed, and multiple consumers can share the work — similar to Kafka.

questions.title: Redis Performance and Eviction
questions.question: How do you configure Redis memory management and eviction policies for optimal performance?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- maxmemory: cap total Redis memory — required for cache use
- Eviction policies: allkeys-lru (evict any key, least recently used), volatile-lru (only keys with TTL), allkeys-lfu (least frequently used, Redis 4+)
- For pure cache: allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu
- For session store: volatile-lru or volatile-ttl
- OBJECT ENCODING: check actual encoding (ziplist, listpack vs hashtable) for memory optimization
- Small hashes/sets/lists use memory-efficient encodings automatically
- SCAN vs KEYS: never use KEYS in production — blocks Redis; use SCAN for iterating

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When using Redis as a cache, always set maxmemory and an eviction policy. Without a maxmemory limit, Redis will consume all available RAM until the server runs out of memory and either crashes or starts swapping, making it extremely slow. With maxmemory and an eviction policy, Redis automatically removes less-used entries when it hits the memory limit.

For a pure cache use case, allkeys-lru is the standard choice. It evicts the least recently used key across all keys when Redis hits its memory limit. This behaves like a classic LRU cache. allkeys-lfu (Least Frequently Used) is often better for skewed access patterns where a small set of keys is accessed very frequently — LFU will keep the hot keys and evict the rarely-accessed ones even if they were recently accessed.

Never use the KEYS command in production. KEYS is O(n) and blocks the entire Redis server while it scans all keys. On a Redis instance with millions of keys, this causes seconds of latency for all other clients. Always use SCAN, which iterates in small batches without blocking.

speakable_v2.hook: When using Redis as a cache, always set maxmemory and an eviction policy.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Always use SCAN, which iterates in small batches without blocking.

questions.title: Redis Eviction Policies and Memory Management
questions.question: How does Redis handle memory limits and what eviction policy should you configure?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- maxmemory: hard cap on Redis memory use — eviction triggers when reached
- Eviction policies: noeviction (error), allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-lfu, allkeys-random, volatile-ttl
- LRU: Least Recently Used — evict least recently accessed key
- LFU: Least Frequently Used — evict least frequently accessed key (better for non-uniform access)
- volatile-*: only evict keys that have a TTL set
- allkeys-lru: recommended for pure cache use case
- volatile-lru: if mixing cache + persistent data in same Redis instance
- Monitor: INFO memory, OBJECT FREQ for LFU, OBJECT IDLETIME for LRU

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Redis eviction policy determines what happens when Redis hits its memory limit. The default is noeviction — Redis returns an error on new writes instead of evicting anything. This is safe for data persistence but terrible for a cache, where you want Redis to automatically make room for new data.

For a pure cache where all keys have TTLs, allkeys-lru is the standard choice. When memory is full, Redis evicts the least recently accessed key — which is the one least likely to be needed again. LFU is better when access patterns are highly non-uniform: a key accessed once months ago looks the same as a new key under LRU, but under LFU the old key would be evicted first.

If you use the same Redis instance for both cache data and session or queue data that you don't want evicted, use volatile-lru. It only evicts keys that have a TTL set, leaving keys without TTL intact. But the cleaner approach is separate Redis instances for different use cases.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Redis Configuration

```bash
# redis.conf or redis-server flags
maxmemory 1gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
# allkeys-lru: evict least recently accessed key from ALL keys
# volatile-lru: evict least recently accessed key from KEYS WITH TTL ONLY
# allkeys-lfu: evict least frequently accessed key
# allkeys-random: evict random key (rarely useful)
# volatile-ttl: evict key with closest expiry
# noeviction: return error (DEFAULT — bad for cache)

# LFU tuning
lfu-decay-time 1         # halve frequency counter every 1 minute
lfu-log-factor 10        # higher = slower counter growth (be selective)
```

## Docker Compose Config

```yaml
redis:
  image: redis:7-alpine
  command: >
    redis-server
    --maxmemory 512mb
    --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
    --save ""
    --appendonly no
  # --save "" and --appendonly no: disable persistence for pure cache
  # Enabling persistence while evicting can cause data inconsistency
```

## Monitor Memory

```bash
# Redis CLI memory inspection
redis-cli INFO memory
# used_memory_human: 245.32M  — actual memory used
# mem_fragmentation_ratio: 1.5 — fragmentation (healthy: 1.0-1.5)
# maxmemory_human: 512.00M   — limit
# evicted_keys: 12345         — number of evicted keys (should be non-zero for caches)

# Check LRU idle time for specific key
redis-cli OBJECT IDLETIME mykey  # seconds since last access

# Check LFU frequency
redis-cli OBJECT FREQ mykey  # frequency counter value
```

## Eviction Policy Decision Tree

```
All data is cache? (can be rebuilt from DB)
  └─ YES → allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu
          (lfu better if some keys very hot, others cold)
  └─ NO  → Do you mix cache + persistent keys in same Redis?
            └─ YES → volatile-lru (cache keys have TTL, persistent keys don't)
            └─ NO  → Use separate Redis instances for cache vs persistence
```

speakable_v2.cap: But the cleaner approach is separate Redis instances for different use cases.

questions.title: Redis High Availability — Sentinel and Cluster
questions.question: What is the difference between Redis Sentinel and Redis Cluster, and how do you connect Spring Boot to each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Sentinel: HA for single Redis instance — automatic failover when master fails; no sharding
- Sentinel monitors master, promotes replica on failure, updates clients with new master address
- Cluster: sharding + HA — data partitioned across multiple masters with replicas
- Cluster: 16384 hash slots distributed across masters; client routes to correct master by key hash
- Sentinel: simpler, good for <10GB data
- Cluster: horizontal scaling, handles larger datasets and higher throughput
- Spring Boot: spring.redis.sentinel.* or spring.redis.cluster.* configuration
- AWS ElastiCache: Sentinel = Primary with Read Replicas; Cluster = Cluster Mode Enabled

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Redis Sentinel provides high availability for a single Redis primary. Three or more Sentinel processes monitor the primary. If the primary becomes unreachable, a quorum of Sentinels agree it's down and elect a replica to be the new primary. Applications configured to use Sentinel automatically discover the current primary address — no manual reconfiguration needed during failover.

Redis Cluster adds horizontal sharding on top of HA. Data is partitioned across multiple primary nodes using hash slots. A cluster of 3 primaries each handles one third of the keyspace, with each primary having a replica for HA. This allows you to scale beyond what a single Redis instance can handle in terms of memory and throughput.

For most Spring Boot applications that use Redis for caching and session storage, Sentinel is the right choice. The data set is manageable on a single instance, and Sentinel provides the automatic failover you need for production. If you're using Redis for real-time analytics with hundreds of GB of data, or need throughput beyond what a single primary can handle, then Cluster is appropriate.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Sentinel Architecture

```
Sentinel 1  Sentinel 2  Sentinel 3
     │            │            │
     └────────────┴────────────┘
              monitor
                  │
          [Redis Master]
               │
         [Redis Replica]  ← promoted to master on failure
```

## Spring Boot Sentinel Configuration

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      sentinel:
        master: mymaster        # master name (configured in sentinel.conf)
        nodes:
          - sentinel1:26379     # Sentinel node addresses
          - sentinel2:26379
          - sentinel3:26379
        password: ${SENTINEL_PASSWORD}
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD}
      timeout: 2000             # connection timeout ms
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 20
          max-idle: 10
          min-idle: 5
```

## Redis Cluster Architecture

```
16384 hash slots distributed across 3 primaries:
Primary A: slots  0-5460   → Replica A
Primary B: slots 5461-10922 → Replica B
Primary C: slots 10923-16383 → Replica C

key → CRC16(key) % 16384 → determines which primary handles it
```

## Spring Boot Cluster Configuration

```yaml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      cluster:
        nodes:
          - redis-1:6379
          - redis-2:6379
          - redis-3:6379
        max-redirects: 3    # follow MOVED/ASK redirects
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD}
      lettuce:
        cluster:
          refresh:
            adaptive: true      # auto-refresh topology on cluster changes
            period: 60s
```

## AWS ElastiCache Mapping

```
ElastiCache for Redis:
  Cluster Mode Disabled = one Primary + Replicas (Sentinel-like HA)
  Cluster Mode Enabled  = Redis Cluster (sharding + HA)

Spring Boot connects to:
  Cluster Mode Disabled: single primary endpoint (AWS handles failover)
  Cluster Mode Enabled:  cluster configuration endpoint
```

speakable_v2.hook: Redis Sentinel provides high availability for a single Redis primary.
speakable_v2.cap: If you're using Redis for real-time analytics with hundreds of GB of data, or need throughput beyond what a single primary can handle, then Cluster is appropriate.
